newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin still firmly in control, says spokesman.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin still firmly in control, says spokesman.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary said on Tuesday the Kremlin leader was firmly in control of Russia despite limits on his activities because of poor health and preparations for heart surgery.

"The president's working ability is limited now by the process of preparing for the operation," Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a Kremlin news briefing, referring to planned bypass surgery to improve the blood supply to Yeltsin's heart.
But he said Yeltsin was working with documents and meeting top officials in the Central Clinical Hospital where he is staying pending the operation.

Yeltsin met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin earlier on Tuesday. Yastrzhembsky said the meeting lasted more than half an hour and that the two discussed a range of crucial issues in Russia's internal and foreign policy.
But a brief television clip of Yeltsin's meeting with Chernomyrdin, released by a Russian television pool, undermined Yastrzhembsky's assurances.
Yeltsin barely moved and appeared to have difficulty in working out what to say. He was shown speaking only a few disjointed words.
One sentence ended with "...council of doctors, operation...", but it was not clear if these were edited fragments of a fuller tape.

Yeltsin has been in hospital for 10 days while doctors prepare him for the operation. A council of doctors is due to meet on Wednesday to decide when to operate and determine the scope of the surgery.
Yastrzhembsky said that while awaiting the doctor's verdict Yeltsin spent between 30 minutes and 2-1/2 hours a day working with documents delivered from his Kremlin office.

"Every day a thick package with documents, which demand (Yeltsin's) attention, is delivered from the Kremlin," he said. "Depending on the urgency of specific issues the package contains between 20 and 70 documents."

Yastrzhembsky made clear his remarks were prompted by an article in Monday's issue of the British newspaper Financial Times which said Yeltsin had a 50:50 chance of surviving the proposed heart operation and could work only 15 minutes a day.
The spokesman issued a statement on Monday which blamed the article for pushing down Russian debt prices in London and said it was wrong from beginning to end.

The Financial Times quoted unspecified Kremlin sources as saying Yeltsin had suffered a stroke as well as a heart attack between the two rounds of the presidential election in June and July and that since then he had been unable to sign documents.
The front-page report said his chief-of-staff, Anatoly Chubais, signed documents for the president using a rubber signature stamp.

Russian debt took a nosedive on international markets on Monday on fears about Yeltsin's health, reversing the euphoria of early last week set off by hopes that Russia would soon receive a good credit rating for its forthcoming first Eurobond.
Russian shares and bonds also fell.
